subject: biology
title: Vaccines
summary: How vaccines train the immune system, primary and secondary responses, how herd immunity protects communities, and why antibiotics differ from vaccines and lose effect through resistance.
body:
A **vaccine** is a preparation that trains the immune system to recognise a pathogen without the person having to suffer the disease first. Vaccination programs have made once-common diseases such as polio and measles rare in many countries. Understanding how vaccines work also helps explain why antibiotics are a completely different tool, and why their overuse is a growing problem.

## Key ideas

### How a vaccine works

A vaccine contains **antigens** from a pathogen, or instructions for body cells to make them, but it cannot cause the full disease. Common types include:

- **Inactivated (killed)** pathogens.
- **Live attenuated** (weakened) pathogens that can no longer cause serious illness in healthy people.
- **Subunit** vaccines containing only part of the pathogen, such as a surface protein.
- **Toxoid** vaccines containing an inactivated toxin (for example, tetanus).
- **mRNA** vaccines, which give cells instructions to make one harmless pathogen protein for a short time.

After vaccination, the immune system responds to the antigens as if they were a real infection. B cells that match the antigen divide, make antibodies and, importantly, form **memory cells**. If the real pathogen enters the body later, these memory cells respond quickly. This is called **artificial active immunity**: active because your own body makes the antibodies and memory cells, and artificial because it was triggered by a vaccine rather than catching the disease.

### Primary and secondary responses

The **primary response** is the immune response the first time the body meets an antigen. It is slow, because only a few B cells match the antigen at first, and they need time to multiply. Antibody levels rise slowly and stay fairly low. During this time a person who has caught the real disease may become ill.

The **secondary response** happens when the same antigen is met again. Because memory cells are already present, the response is:

- **faster** (antibodies appear sooner)
- **larger** (antibody levels rise much higher)
- **longer lasting**.

A vaccine produces the primary response safely. Then, when the real pathogen arrives, the body gives a secondary response and usually destroys it before symptoms develop. Some vaccines need **booster** doses, which are extra doses given later to make the secondary response stronger and keep memory cell numbers up.

### Herd immunity

**Herd immunity** (also called community immunity) is the indirect protection that happens when a large proportion of a population is immune to an infectious disease. If most people cannot catch and pass on the pathogen, it has trouble finding new hosts, so chains of transmission break.

This protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies too young for some vaccines or people whose immune systems are weakened by illness or treatment. The proportion of people who need to be immune differs between diseases. Diseases that spread very easily, such as measles, need a very high proportion of the population to be immune. If vaccination rates fall, outbreaks can return.

### Vaccines versus antibiotics

Vaccines and antibiotics are often confused, but they do different jobs:

| Feature | Vaccine | Antibiotic |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Prevents disease | Treats an existing infection |
| Works by | Training the immune system to make memory cells | Killing bacteria or stopping them from growing |
| Works against | Bacteria or viruses (depending on the vaccine) | Bacteria only |
| When it is used | Before infection | After infection |

An **antibiotic** is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them reproducing, often by damaging their cell wall or interfering with processes that human cells do not have. Antibiotics do **not** work on viruses, because viruses have no cell wall or cell processes of their own. Taking antibiotics for a cold or the flu will not help.

### Antibiotic resistance

**Antibiotic resistance** is when bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic that used to work. It develops by **natural selection**:

1. In a large population of bacteria, there is variation. By chance, a few bacteria may have a mutation that lets them survive the antibiotic.
2. When the antibiotic is used, the non-resistant bacteria die.
3. The resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance gene.
4. Over time, most of the population is resistant, and the antibiotic stops working.

The antibiotic does not create the mutation. It only gives the resistant bacteria an advantage. Resistance is made more likely by overusing antibiotics (for example, for viral infections), not finishing a prescribed course as directed, and heavy use in farm animals. Ways to slow it include only using antibiotics when needed, following the doctor's instructions, good hygiene and vaccination, which means fewer infections need treating.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Interpreting an antibody graph

**Scenario:** A child is given a vaccine on day 0 and a booster on day 60. Antibody levels rise slightly between days 7 and 20, then fall. After the booster, levels rise within a few days to a level much higher than the first peak. Explain the shape of the graph.

**Step 1:** The first dose triggers the primary response. Few B cells match, so antibodies appear slowly and peak at a low level.
**Step 2:** Memory cells are formed during this primary response.
**Step 3:** The booster contains the same antigen. Memory cells recognise it straight away, causing a secondary response.

**Answer:** The second rise is faster and higher because memory cells from the first dose produced a secondary response.

### Example 2: Explaining resistance

**Scenario:** A farm uses an antibiotic regularly in animal feed. After some years, an infection in the animals no longer responds to that antibiotic. Explain what happened.

**Step 1:** The bacterial population contained variation, including a few bacteria with a resistance mutation.
**Step 2:** Regular antibiotic use killed the non-resistant bacteria, leaving the resistant ones.
**Step 3:** These survived, reproduced and passed on resistance, so the population became mostly resistant.

**Answer:** Natural selection favoured resistant bacteria because of repeated antibiotic exposure.

## Common mistakes

- Saying a vaccine "contains antibodies". Most vaccines contain antigens (or instructions for making them); your body makes the antibodies.
- Thinking antibiotics kill viruses. They only work against bacteria.
- Saying the antibiotic "causes" bacteria to mutate or "become used to" it. Resistant bacteria already existed and were selected.
- Saying people become resistant to antibiotics. It is the bacteria that become resistant.
- Believing herd immunity means everyone is vaccinated. It means enough people are immune to stop the pathogen spreading easily.

## Exam tips

- In graph questions, name the primary and secondary responses and link the secondary response to memory cells.
- For resistance, write the natural selection steps in order: variation, selection, survival, reproduction, inheritance.
- When comparing vaccines and antibiotics, give a clear difference in both purpose (prevent or treat) and target (immune system or bacteria).

## Key terms

- **Vaccine** — a preparation of antigens (or instructions for making them) that triggers immunity without causing the disease.
- **Primary response** — the slower, smaller immune response to the first exposure to an antigen.
- **Secondary response** — the faster, larger response to a later exposure, due to memory cells.
- **Booster** — an extra vaccine dose that strengthens immunity.
- **Artificial active immunity** — immunity in which your body makes its own antibodies and memory cells in response to a vaccine.
- **Herd immunity** — indirect protection of a population when enough people are immune.
- **Antibiotic** — a medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth.
- **Antibiotic resistance** — the ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic that once killed them.
- **Natural selection** — the process in which individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more.

## Summary

- Vaccines expose the immune system to harmless antigens so memory cells form.
- The primary response is slow and small; the secondary response is fast and large.
- Herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated by breaking chains of transmission.
- Vaccines prevent disease; antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do not affect viruses.
- Antibiotic resistance spreads by natural selection and is worsened by overuse.

questions.prompt: What does a typical vaccine contain?

options.C: Antigens from a pathogen, or instructions to make them

questions.explanation: Vaccines provide antigens (or instructions for making them) so your own immune system responds. Option A is a common misconception: in active immunity your body makes the antibodies itself.
Antibiotics target structures and processes found in bacteria, such as the cell wall. Viruses lack these, so option C is wrong even though many people take antibiotics for colds.

questions.prompt: Why does the secondary response protect a vaccinated person from becoming ill?

options.A: The vaccine kills the pathogen as soon as it enters
options.B: Memory cells produce antibodies quickly and in large amounts, destroying the pathogen before symptoms develop
options.D: The pathogen cannot enter the body of a vaccinated person

questions.explanation: Memory cells formed after vaccination allow a fast, large antibody response. Option D is wrong because the pathogen can still enter; it is destroyed quickly once inside.

questions.prompt: How does herd immunity protect a baby too young to be vaccinated?

options.A: The baby receives memory cells from people nearby
options.B: The pathogen becomes weaker in large populations
options.C: Vaccinated people pass antibodies to the baby through the air
options.D: Most people around the baby are immune, so the pathogen is less likely to reach the baby

questions.explanation: When most people are immune, the pathogen struggles to find new hosts and chains of transmission break. Option A is wrong because memory cells are not passed between people in this way.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antibiotic resistance is correct?

options.A: Antibiotics cause bacteria to mutate so they can survive
options.B: People's bodies become resistant to antibiotics
options.C: Resistant bacteria already present survive and reproduce when the antibiotic is used

questions.explanation: Resistance develops by natural selection of bacteria that already had a resistance mutation. Option A is tempting, but antibiotics do not create mutations; they select for them.

questions.prompt: A patient asks for antibiotics for the flu, which is caused by a virus. What is the best advice?

options.A: Antibiotics will not help, and unnecessary use encourages antibiotic resistance
options.B: Antibiotics will help if taken early
options.C: Antibiotics will prevent the flu from spreading to others
options.D: Antibiotics will boost the immune system

questions.explanation: Antibiotics do not affect viruses, and using them unnecessarily selects for resistant bacteria in the body. Option B is wrong because timing does not change the fact that viruses are not affected.

questions.prompt: A graph shows antibody levels after two doses of the same vaccine. Which description matches the second dose?

options.A: Slower rise and lower peak than the first dose
options.C: Same speed and same peak as the first dose
options.D: Faster rise and higher peak than the first dose

questions.explanation: The second dose triggers a secondary response because memory cells are present, so antibodies rise faster and higher. Option C ignores the effect of memory cells.

questions.prompt: In a town, measles vaccination rates fall over several years. What is the most likely result?

options.A: Measles bacteria become resistant to antibiotics
options.B: Herd immunity weakens, so outbreaks of measles become more likely
options.C: Unvaccinated people develop memory cells naturally without infection

questions.explanation: With fewer immune people, the virus can spread more easily and reach those who are not protected. Option A is wrong because measles is caused by a virus, and antibiotic resistance concerns bacteria.
